bib.title: Partial Monitoring (Chapter 37 of Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press (book chapter)

question: How should a learner act when the loss of the chosen action is not directly observed, and when can sublinear regret be achieved in finite adversarial partial monitoring games?
contributions: Classification of finite adversarial partial monitoring games into trivial, easy, hard and hopeless by elementary linear algebra (Theorem 37.11)
Lower bounds for hard, hopeless and easy games
Exponential-weights policy (Algorithm 26) with convex information/regret-balancing exploration, O(sqrt n) for locally and O(n^(2/3)) for globally observable games

results.claim: Matching pennies with costly feedback (c>1/2) forces regret of order n^(2/3) on any policy.
results.setup: Example 37.3: k=3 actions (heads, tails, uncertain), d=2 outcomes, known cost c>1/2; lower bound via randomised adversary p=1/2+-eps, eps=n^(-1/3)
results.quote: Matching pennies is a hard game for c > 1/2 in the sense that the adversary can force the regret of any policy to be at least Ω(n2/3).

results.claim: Classification theorem: finite adversarial partial-monitoring games have minimax regret 0, Theta(n^1/2), Theta(n^2/3) or Omega(n), and nothing else.
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)
results.setup: Finite adversarial game G=(L,Phi); trivial if no neighbouring actions; easy if locally observable with neighbours; hard if globally but not locally observable; hopeless otherwise
results.quote: A partial monitoring game is called trivial if R∗ n(G) = 0, easy if R∗ n(G) = Θ(n1/2), hard if R∗ n(G) = Θ(n2/3) and hopeless if R∗ n(G) = Ω(n).
results.note: Theorem is from Bartok et al. 2014 (non-degenerate) and Lattimore & Szepesvari 2019a (degenerate), per Sec 37.10

results.claim: Hard games lower bound: globally observable but not locally observable games have minimax regret at least c_G n^(2/3).
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)
results.setup: Theorem 37.12; c_G>0 game-dependent constant; proof by two stochastic alternatives u_a, u_b indistinguishable via Nab, Delta ~ n^(-1/3)
results.quote: Then there exists a constant cG > 0 such that R∗ n(G) ≥cGn2/3.

results.claim: Hopeless games: not globally observable with at least two non-dominated actions gives linear minimax regret.
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)
results.setup: Theorem 37.13 (left as exercise; proof sketch given)
results.quote: then there exists a constant cG > 0 such that R∗ n(G) ≥cGn.

results.claim: Easy games lower bound: locally observable games with a neighbouring pair have minimax regret at least c_G sqrt(n) for large n.
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)

results.claim: Algorithm 26 (exponential weights with information-regret balanced exploration) regret bound for any eta>0, eps>0.
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)
results.setup: Globally observable game, losses in [0,1]; Qt exp-weights on Pareto optimal actions, Pt solves Eq. 37.12

results.claim: Locally observable games: tuned Algorithm 26 gets sqrt(n) regret with k^(3/2) dependence.
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)
results.setup: From Thm 37.15 + 37.17 with opt*(eta)<=9k^3 max(1,v_loc^2) for eta<=1/(2k^2 max(1,v_loc))

results.claim: Globally observable games: tuned Algorithm 26 gets n^(2/3) regret.
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)
results.setup: From Thm 37.15 + 37.16 with opt*(eta)<=2 v_glo k^2/sqrt(eta) for eta<=1/max{1,v_glo^2 k^4}

results.claim: v_glo and v_loc can be exponentially large in d.
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)
results.value: v <= d^(1/2) k^(d/2); v_loc<=m if locally observable and non-degenerate

results.claim: Algorithm 26 recovers bandit bound: opt*(eta)<=k/2 for bandit games (Phi=L).
results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)
results.setup: Proposition 37.19(a); consistent with Exp3 O(sqrt(kn log k))

results.source: Lattimore & Szepesvari, Bandit Algorithms ch. 37 (cites original papers in remarks)

results.claim: Adversarial bandits with binary losses: Exp3 regret O(sqrt(kn log k)); sqrt(kn) is optimal up to constant.
results.source: Ch. 11 and Exercise 15.4 of same book
results.quote: guarantees a regret of O( p kn log(k)),

results.claim: Matching pennies with c=1/4: transferring mass to the revealing action makes the stability term at most 1/2(1/2+1) vs 1/(32)+(1-eps)/(4 eps) unbounded.
results.setup: Section 37.7 worked example, L,Phi of Example 37.3 with c=1/4, q=(1/2-eps/2,1/2-eps/2,eps)
results.quote: p = q −min(q1, q2)(e1 + e2) + 2 min(q1, q2)e3 .
results.note: Naive estimator gives (1/32+(1-eps)/(4 eps)); text extraction of fraction is garbled

results.claim: Piccolboni & Schindelhauer 2001 first non-asymptotic result: O(n^3/4) for globally observable; Cesa-Bianchi et al. 2006 reduced to O(n^2/3); Foster & Rakhlin 2012 first O(n^1/2) for non-degenerate locally observable.
results.quote: derive a policy with regret O(n3/4) for globally observable games.

results.claim: As horizon grows, game dependence diminishes for point-locally observable-type results: limsup R_n/sqrt(n) <= 8(2+m) sqrt(2 k_loc log k).
results.quote: lim sup n→∞ Rn √n ≤8(2 + m) p 2kloc log(k) .

results.claim: Chaudhuri & Tewari 2016: linear globally observable setting with explore-then-commit gives O(n^2/3 log n) regret.
results.quote: prove O(n2/3 log(n)) regret using an explore-then-commit algorithm.

limits: The Landau notation hides dependence on k, d, m and finer structure of G (Sec 37.3).
vglo and vloc depend only on G but may be exponentially large in d (Prop 37.18).
Note 14: 'Partial monitoring is still quite poorly understood'; dependence of regret on d, k, m is mostly unknown and lower bounds are 'surely very conservative'.
opt*(eta) may be hard to compute since q -> opt_q(eta) is not convex; Note 7 gives adaptive learning rate; Note 9: numerical instability for small eta or large k, d.
Contextual version not covered; infinite action/outcome settings not systematically studied (Note 11).
Problem-dependent regret in the in-between regime between minimax and asymptotic is open (Note 5).
Foster-Rakhlin 2012 and Bartok 2013 core proofs contain errors per Sec 37.10.
practices: Reduce the search for the optimal action to Pareto optimal actions and estimate only loss differences between neighbouring ones, chained along a path (Sec 37.2.2).
Classify a game by checking neighbour pairs for global and local observability: existence of f with sum_c f(c,Phi_ci)=L_ai-L_bi (Eq. 37.3), restricted to Nab for local (Sec 37.2.2).
In hard games the learner must play badly suboptimal actions to gain information, so pay exploration only when needed (Sec 37.2.2).
Use importance-weighted loss-difference estimators f(A,sigma)/p_A with exploration distribution P_t chosen by a convex program rather than fixed epsilon-greedy (Sec 37.5).
Use adaptive learning rate eta_t=min(1/B, sqrt(log k/(1+sum V_s))) to avoid computing opt*(eta) (Note 7).
Application guidance: costly-information settings (spam labelling by human, medical tests, factory quality testing, dynamic pricing) are partial monitoring problems (Note 10).

terms.definition: A finite, k-action, d-outcome adversarial partial monitoring problem is specified by a loss matrix L in R^{k x d} and a feedback matrix Phi in Sigma^{k x d}, where Sigma is called the set of signals; learner receives sigma_t=Phi_{A_t i_t}, loss y_ta=L_{a i_t}; m is the maximum number of distinct symbols in any row of Phi.
Partial monitoring problem where Phi=L, learner observes the loss of the chosen action.
Phi_ai=i for all a and i; signal reveals the losses for all actions.
Minimax regret R*_n(G)=0 / Theta(n^1/2) / Theta(n^2/3) / Omega(n).
C_a={u in P_{d-1}: max_b <l_a-l_b,u> <= 0}, the set of outcome distributions where action a is optimal; a convex polytope.

terms.term: Dominated, Pareto optimal, degenerate, duplicate actions
terms.definition: Dominated: C_a empty. Pareto optimal: dimension d-1. Degenerate: non-dominated with lower dimension. Duplicates: l_a=l_b. Game is degenerate if it has any degenerate or duplicate actions.
Pareto optimal a,b are neighbours if C_a ∩ C_b has dimension d-2; N_ab={c: C_a ∩ C_b subset C_c}; graph over [k] with edges between neighbours.
Neighbours a,b for which exists f: [k]xSigma->R with sum_c f(c,Phi_ci)=L_ai-L_bi for all i (Eq. 37.3).
As global, but f(c,sigma)=0 whenever c not in N_ab.
Two feedback matrices encode the same information if the pattern of identical entries in each row match.
Inf over f in E^vec and p of max_i [ (1/eta)(p-q)^T L e_i + (1/eta^2) sum_a p_a Psi_q(eta f(a,Phi_ai)/p_a) ]; opt* is sup over q supported on Pareto optimal actions.
Vector y constant on duplicates and increasing in the direction of the in-tree arrows; Lemma 37.20 maps q to r, T-increasing with r>=q/k and <r-q,y><=0 for T-decreasing y.

code.snippet: Input: eta, eps, L, Phi. for t in 1..n: Q_ta = I_Pi(a) exp(-eta sum_{s<t} yhat_sa) / sum_{b in Pi} exp(-eta sum_{s<t} yhat_sb); solve Eq. 37.12 with q=Q_t, precision eps for P_t, f_t in E^vec; sample A_t ~ P_t, observe sigma_t; set yhat_t = f_t(A_t, sigma_t)/P_{tA_t}
sum_{c=1}^k f(c, Phi_ci) = L_ai - L_bi  for all i in [d]
